newsitem.title: USA: Mich school funding to state supreme court, again.
newsitem.headline: Mich school funding to state supreme court, again.

text.p: The Michigan Supreme Court on Thursday is scheduled to hear oral arguments in a 17-year-old school funding lawsuit that could cost the state anywhere from $600 million to more than $3.5 billion.

It will be the fourth time the state supreme court entertains arguments from attorneys in the longrunning litigation, this time an appeal from a $492 million judgment entered in favor of 84 school districts.
The justices had first declined to hear an appeal from the judgment, but reversed themselves last November after a plea from Gov. John Engler.
With interest, the judgment entered then now totals more than $600 million for the school districts, said plaintiff's attorney Dennis Pollard.
In September 1995, a state appeals court essentially found that Michigan had not been meeting its constitutional funding requirements particularly in the area of special education.
The central question Thursday, then, is whether the state or the federal government has mandated special education programs in Michigan, Pollard said.

If it is the federal government, as state officials contend, then Michigan does not have to provide full funding for the programs. If it is a state mandate, however, then the Michigan constitution requires full state funding, Pollard said.

The appeals court has held that the special education programs, while mandated by the federal government for funding, were in fact created as a requirement by the state of Michigan and therefore must be funded by the state.
"They have dodged a bullet for all these years and its come to a reckoning," Pollard said.
The governor recognizes that the state holds some liability for funding the school programs, but objects to Michgian being held liable for the whole amount, spokesman John Truscott said.
In pursing these appeals, the state seeks "recognition from the Supreme Court that many of the mandates came from the federal government, not the state," Truscott said.
"We admit there is some liability, but the state instituted these programs pursuant to a federal mandate,'' Truscott said.

Michigan has a very strict constitutional requirement for state funding, but the state shouldn't be held responsible for federal mandates when it wasn't the original source for the programs, Truscott said.

The initial rejection of the appeal led the state to cap spending, enact a hiring freeze and eliminate some capital spending projects, said Maureen McNulty, a spokeswoman for the state's budget office.

If upheld, the judgment has far broader implications than just for the school districts participating, McNulty said. If the decision stands, and is applied to all the state's school districts with retroactive and future claims, it could cost the state more than $3.5 billion, she said.
